body:
For this case, can't the user enable real nested transactions?

We already discussed the problems of throwing exceptions, and in the context of the ORM they could potentially cause more harm than it would help.

> For this case, can't the user enable real nested transactions?

Not all databases support nested transactions.

> We already discussed the problems of throwing exceptions, and in the context of the ORM they could potentially cause more harm than it would help.

I would like to hear that. What is the harm?
For databases that don't support nested transactions it doesn't look like we can easily emulate nested transactions either. We don't have many options other than an exception at that point.

The harm of exception is that they leave inconsistent state behind when not caught. We have many places during the save process where we don't catch exceptions. In those places, we would need to catch this new exception in order to keep operating as usual.

A database record being persisted despite that you would assume it should not due to *failing* transactions sounds very harmful. When using `->transactional(function() {})` I would assume that either everything inside works or fails and not something in between.

But a rollback is not unusual, it is something you can expect. A PDO error is something that is out of your control. As I said in the slack channel, we only need to make sure to catch the exception in the methods that are invoked by the save process. The will make things work the same as before, but people can still have the exception if they need it.

@lorenzo I may understand your concern a little bit. Then I have another approach and now I think this idea might be better.

```sql
// Allowed nest types
BEGIN
    (BEGIN)
    (COMMIT)
COMMIT

BEGIN
   (BEGIN)
   (COMMIT)
ROLLBACK

BEGIN
   (BEGIN)
   (ROLLBACK)
ROLLBACK

// Not allowed nest type
BEGIN
   (BEGIN)
   (ROLLBACK)
COMMIT // Error. Throw an exception.
```
In this idea, the `rollback()` call of the last type doesn't throw an exception really, but marks the transaction as it should be failed. And if people call `commit()` after that, then it throws NestedTransactionRollbackException. However, if people call `rollback()` as failure operation, like the third example, it doesn't throw anything.

What do you think about this idea?

@chinpei215 I like the idea! While it does not solve the problem, it will at least inform the user during the testing phase that there is something wrong with their logic.

A complete solution to this problem would require a very different design of the ORM, but I think we can mitigate it with different strategies.

Another strategy we can use after implementing you idea is to keep some state in the connection that can be used by the ORM to know when it was expecting to be inside a transaction and where it does not. This way, we can prevent calls to `insert()` `update()` or `delete()` if we can detect that the ORM was expecting to be inside a transaction but in reality it was closed.

Fortunately this is not a problem for postgres users :)

@lorenzo Thank you. I should have shown you this idea first. I think now we have some consensus for fixing the issue. As a first step, we could throw a new exception when the most outer transaction was closed, if some inconsistent operation - `commit()` after `rollback()`, was done in it. And, as the second step, we can improve the ORM to suppress `insert()`, `update()` or `delete()` calls if the transaction should be failed. I can do the first enhancement. I would like to put it on the top of my todo list.

The latest MySQL and SQLite also seem to support the SAVEPOINT statement. Maybe, we can change `Connection::$_useSavePoints` to `true` by default in future release? Personally, I have never used the statement though.

Semi-OT
> Fortunately this is not a problem for postgres users :)

Means postgres keeps record on the transaction state and would not allow out of order statements?
